An electrovalent bond, also known as an ionic bond, is a chemical bond formed by the complete transfer of electrons from one atom (usually a metal) to another atom (usually a nonmetal), resulting in the formation of oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction.
Ionic compounds show anisotropic properties. · Ionic Bond Formation of MgCl, > Mg 2[Cls] or MgCl Mg"* + 2CIl—> Mg**2CI" or MgCl, Lewis Dot Structure of MgCl, (electron dot structures)
Properties of Ionic Compounds

1. Physical Nature: Jonic compounds are hard crystalline solids because of strong force of attraction between the positive and negative ions. These compounds are generally brittle and break into pieces when pressure is applied.
Melting and boiling points: These compounds have high melting and boiling points as large amount of energy is required to break strong inter-ionic attraction.
Solubility: These compounds are soluble in water (polar solvent) and insoluble in organic solvents (non- polar solvent) like kerosene, benzene, ether, petrol, etc.

Conduction of electricity: The conduction of electricity through a solution involves movement of charged particle. Ionic and electrovalent compounds are good conductors of electricity, but they conduct electricity either in molten form or in their aqueous solution, as the ions are free to move and carry charge.

It is a process that uses electricity to purify impure metals. An impure metal is used as anode and a pure metal is used as cathode. A solution of a metal salt is used as electrolyte. When an electric current is passed through the cell, the impure metal dissolves into the electrolyte and is replaced by an equal amount of pure metal from the cathode.
CuSO, solution Anode mud
The pure metal is deposited at the cathode, while the insoluble impurities from the impure metal settle down beneath the anode as anode mud.
